phase2_corrections_to_phase1_metadata: Unit metadata (hr-07-poggeler.json) and Phase 0 overview both state 'continuous prose with NO internal section headings.' This is INCORRECT. The essay has TWO Roman-numeral sections: 'I. THE PATH TO BEING AND TIME' (book p. 164 / PDF p. 170) and 'II. FROM ARISTOTLE TO NIETZSCHE' (book p. 168 / PDF p. 174). The opening 3.5 pages (book 161-164 / PDF 167-170) are an unheaded preamble that establishes the topology-of-being framework. Pöggeler's tripartite structure (preamble + I + II) is, however, distinctive: the preamble is unusually long (~3.5 pp.) and the two body sections are roughly equal (~4.5 + ~4 pp.). The 'continuous prose' description was an artifact of the preamble's prominence.
essay_thesis: Heidegger's serious, sustained engagement with rhetoric is restricted to the Marburg lecture courses of 1923-28, where rhetoric was taken up in the framework of an interpretation of Aristotle and Plato; in his mature thought, the 'topology of being' (Topologie des Seins) — articulated in the 1947 Aus der Erfahrung des Denkens, the 1957 Der Satz vom Grund, and crystallized in the Geviert (fourfold) — supplants the Aristotelian-rhetorical framework with a poetic, place-based discussion (Erörterung) that is no longer rhetorical, even though Heidegger's debt to the rhetorical tradition is hidden but persistent.

sections.heading: [Opening — no heading; introduces topology-of-being as Heidegger's mature concept]
summary_bullets: Opens with the 'troubled year 1947': Heidegger, indicted for Nazi entanglement, privately publishes Aus der Erfahrung des Denkens, in which he separates himself from 'half-poetic reason' and identifies 'thoughtful poetics' with 'the topology of being [Seyn]' — the dwelling-place (Ortschaft) of essence

Tracks Heidegger forward to 1957: Der Satz vom Grund replaces systematic essence-articulation (still operative in the 1929 Husserl Festschrift contribution 'Vom Wesen des Grundes') with a listening-for-language; Heidegger reads the principle of reason via Dilthey (Introduction to the Human Sciences), Leibniz, Hegel, and Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy §15 ('supreme metaphysical delusion')

The 'discussion' (Erörterung) Heidegger now practices is structured by topoi (places); Pöggeler relates this to the rhetorical tradition (topoi as exemplary places), to Curtius's medieval-Latin Toposforschung, and to Auerbach's Mimesis (topology of Western literature; topoi as Leitworte / guiding-words)

Cites Heidegger's December 12, 1958 letter to Pöggeler: 'I use the term "topology" quite literally: the speaking of place; that is, thinking the truth (the disclosure of the self-concealed [das Entbergen des Sichverbergens]) of being [des Seyns]' — Heidegger explicitly distances his usage from 'historical connotations'

Geviert (fourfold) inscribed crosswise with strikethrough on Seyn — this is the literal topographic figure of the topology of being; Pöggeler positions Vico, Viehweg's Topik und Jurisprudenz, Hartmann's dialectic-as-technique, and Karl-Otto Apel's 'linguistic-philosophical bridge building' as parallel attempts; Heidegger is NOT involved in this 'alchemy'

Closes the preamble with a regret: 'It is thus all the more regrettable that Heidegger did not further develop this early exploratory path' — i.e., the rhetorical-topical engagement Heidegger left behind

sections.heading: I. THE PATH TO BEING AND TIME
sections.argumentative_role: first body section: pre-Marburg through Marburg origins of the rhetorical engagement
summary_bullets: Reconstructs Heidegger's intellectual formation: Catholic theologian → Husserlian phenomenology (1916) → reaction to WWI catastrophe → reversal of Husserl's transcendental turn back toward facticity (Faktizität)

Franz Overbeck dissolves the synthesis of antiquity and Christianity for the young Heidegger; original Christianity is eschatological — believers do not strive for Greek wisdom; Heidegger's 1920-21 Introduction to the Phenomenology of Religion (GA 60) interprets the Pauline letters

1922 Natorp-Bericht: Heidegger sketches an Aristotle book (NE VI + Metaphysics + Physics) where phronēsis is characterized as conscience (Gewissen), discrediting metaphysical reason; Luther is enlisted against Aristotelian-Thomist theology

Marburg 1923-28: Heidegger's 1925-26 winter lecture course title shifted from the announced 'Aristotle: Rhetoric' to 'Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy' (i.e., GA 18 SS 1924, n. 28); Heidegger sharpens the Plato/sophist opposition (Sophist course; Plato refuses, Aristotle classifies rhetoric under topics within practical philosophy)

BT (1927) is dedicated to Husserl but indebted to Max Scheler (the realm of the emotional); Heidegger develops fear via Aristotle, links fear to anxiety following the Christian tradition (Stoic 'Nec spe nec metu' contrasted with the Pauline 'fear and trembling' that hope rescues)

Pöggeler's KEY CLAIM, quoting BT §29: Heidegger's gloss — 'Contrary to the traditional orientation of the concept of rhetoric to something like a 'subject,' Aristotle's work must be regarded as the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness (Alltäglichkeit) of being amongst one another' — is read NOT as Heidegger validating rhetoric but as Heidegger CONFINING the political to everydayness (Öffentlichkeit / das Man), since after this acknowledgment Heidegger 'leaves behind not only Aristotle but, for example, Max Scheler as well'; Pöggeler asks whether Heidegger 'restricted crucial dimensions of Aristotle's Rhetoric on the path to Being and Time'
Closes Section I by noting Aristotle and Aquinas both queried the image of justice in 'new rhetoric' (Perelman); Heidegger 'failed to ask this question' — the omission is itself the restriction

sections.heading: II. FROM ARISTOTLE TO NIETZSCHE
sections.argumentative_role: second body section: post-1924 trajectory away from rhetoric toward poetics
summary_bullets: BT presents itself as 'interpretation'; in SS 1924 (GA 18) Heidegger asked PHILOLOGICAL questions about Aristotle's fundamental concepts; humans are simultaneously linguistic and political, 'distinguished through speech from other animals, such as bees' (Aristotle Pol. I.2 — zōon politikon); Aristotle's Rhetoric addresses the polis-orientation toward decisions

The speaker sets out from a shared opinion (endoxon) and returns to it: 'not a matter of scientific proof (apodeixis)' — this is an orientation that, while directed toward truth, depends on the ability to share the opinions (doxa) of others

Speaker characterized by ethos / Haltung (attitude) and pathos / Befindlichkeit (one's feeling of attunement) — Heidegger glosses Greek pathos with the BT existentiale Befindlichkeit; cites Dilthey's Renaissance-and-Reformation analyses; Augustinian distinction between holy fear (timor castus) and slavish fear (timor servilis)

At the close of GA 18, Heidegger asserts movement (kinēsis) possesses both poiētikon (capacity for creativity) and pathētikon (capacity for feeling); from the suggestive brevity of this conclusion, the 'destruction of traditional ontology proceeds from its analysis of manual activity' — praxis becomes poiesis (production), being 'still must cling to the eidos or appearance of being as it presents itself'; the pathetic / feeling is relegated to attunement (Befindlichkeit) and mood (Stimmung)

Heidegger's reading is QUESTIONABLE: how can someone who has carried out a year-long examination of Aristotle not find praxis in the communication of common issues? Plato becomes for Heidegger 'the aristocrat,' Aristotle 'son of a medical doctor' — both wedded to a 2000-year 'ontology of shoemaking' (cited from Scheler's reception); Oskar Becker (Heidegger's first mentor) lexically refuted these readings

Fall 1929 turn to Nietzsche: the destruction of philosophical tradition that BT was to lead to a systematic reconstruction now unfolds in a 'completely new fashion'; reason is unfair to life and history; Hölderlin placed beside Nietzsche; in 1938 'conversion year' Heidegger makes Nietzsche jointly responsible for National Socialism — Nietzsche is 'most excessive metaphysician' of metaphysics' demise; Heidegger fails to respect Nietzsche's listening to the Romantics and theories of irony (Behler's bumping into Nietzsche the rhetorician via Derrida)

Letter on Humanism (1947) — fall 1946: Heidegger differentiates himself from Sartre's existentialism; the elemental shift (Kehre) in thought and existence (Dasein) is announced; humanism of Renaissance derived from Rome (Herder's view rejected); animal rationale relegates the human to the 'level of the animal' — Hölderlin enlisted against 'Goethe's citizen of the world' and the Romantics' approach

1962 Greece trip: Heidegger imagined himself as Heraclitus aboard ship; never alighted on Patmos; isolated cabin-dweller and Naples-inhabit are contradictory worlds — Heidegger's Eigentlichkeit (most personal character) vs. the public-spirited rhetorical tradition; 'Nevertheless the reader cannot get rid of the impression that, even when it is hidden, Heidegger touches the rhetorical tradition again and again'

Cites Samuel Ijsseling (Rhetoric and Philosophy in Conflict): late Heidegger's truth-of-language regards self-concealments from a 'strictly non-Platonic and non-metaphysical standpoint,' yet 'we cannot fail to recognize that Heidegger's concept adheres strictly to the ancient Greek understanding of language, as it is presented, for example, in Isocrates' panegyric on the power of speech and language'

Julius Ebbinghaus correspondence (Nov 22, 1950): Heidegger writes that he might have been 'preoccupied by the field of religious questioning' all along; Ebbinghaus replies on tolerance; 1953 Trakl essay (Merkur) and 1959 On the Way to Language explain that 'discussion (Erörterung) points to place (Ort); and place gathers in and permeates everything'

Closes essay with Ebbinghaus's published draft-letter: discuss (Erörtern) is recent invention from Aristotle's topics — to discuss = to carry contemplation through prescribed places (Örter/loci); 'For this reason, woodpaths (Holzwege) do not mean wood paths because wood is an old word for forest, but because they are paths that have been driven through a wood to carry out timber' — woodpaths end blind where timber has been made and taken — paths that DECEIVE the traveler

Final paragraph — Pöggeler's verdict: 'Is it sad if philosophers follow diverse paths, eventually being able at best to wave to one another across the intervening distance?'; 'Perhaps it is the nature of philosophy that we all proceed from different places on the periphery, aiming at a common center, while still remaining bound by the prejudices of our time to our starting point on that periphery, in our thinking and in our politics'; 'Rhetoric seeks to follow up such binding and development. Heidegger made remarkable contributions to this search, but did not exhaust its tradition and its future possibilities.'

key_concepts.name: Topology of Being
key_concepts.german_form: Topologie des Seins (also Seyn with crosswise strikethrough)
key_concepts.english_form: topology of being / topology of Being / dwelling-place of essence
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's mature post-1947 concept (introduced in Aus der Erfahrung des Denkens, glossed in his Dec 12, 1958 letter to Pöggeler): the 'literal speaking of place,' 'thinking the truth' as 'the disclosure of the self-concealed (Entbergen des Sichverbergens) of being.' This is the place-figure that supplants both metaphysical essence-articulation and the Aristotelian-rhetorical engagement of the Marburg years. Crystallized in the Geviert (fourfold: earth, sky, mortal, gods).

key_concepts.name: Restricted Conception of Rhetoric
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Pöggeler's titular thesis: Heidegger's serious engagement with rhetoric is circumscribed to the Marburg lectures of 1923-28 (especially GA 18 SS 1924), where rhetoric was thematized in an interpretation of Aristotle within practical philosophy and contrasted to Plato's anti-rhetoric. 'Restricted' here means BOTH temporally bounded (not central to either pre-Marburg formation or post-1928 mature thought) AND substantively curtailed (Heidegger 'restricted crucial dimensions of Aristotle's Rhetoric on the path to Being and Time' — failing to ask after justice; relegating pathos to Befindlichkeit; surrendering rhetoric to the 'they').

key_concepts.name: Discussion (Erörterung)
key_concepts.english_form: discussion (with the constitutive sense of bringing-into-place)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's term for what the topology of being practices. The German Erörterung (from Ort, place) cannot be rendered in English without losing the place-figure (translator's note 46). 'Discussion (Erörterung) points to place (Ort); and place gathers in and permeates everything' (cited from the 1953 Trakl essay / 1959 On the Way to Language). It is the post-rhetorical practice — listening for language rather than systematically articulating essence — that Heidegger develops from 1957 onward.

key_concepts.name: Geviert (Fourfold)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's mature topographic figure (introduced in essays on Thought and Poetry written 1941-47, n. 12); the four corners (earth, sky, mortal, gods) cross over Seyn (Being with strikethrough), making the topology of being literally a place-figure. The Geviert is the geometric realization of the post-rhetorical, post-metaphysical 'thinking the truth.'

key_concepts.name: Topoi as Guiding-Words (Leitworte)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: From the rhetorical-literary tradition (Curtius, Auerbach Mimesis): topoi are exemplary places that orient remembrance and provide materials for trains of thought. Auerbach's 'topology' identifies guiding-words (Leitworte) lexically extractable from texts (e.g., 'la cour et la ville' for the French classics). Pöggeler holds out the rhetorical topos-as-Leitwort as the BACKGROUND tradition Heidegger's Topologie partly inhabits without acknowledging.

key_concepts.name: Phronēsis as Conscience
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's 1922 Natorp-Bericht move: phronēsis (NE VI) is characterized as conscience (Gewissen), thereby 'discrediting metaphysical reason' and putting NE VI in tension with Metaphysics Theta. Pöggeler treats this as the conceptually decisive translation that channels the rhetorical-pathos register into the ethical-existential register of BT.

key_concepts.name: Pathos as Befindlichkeit (Attunement)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's gloss in GA 18: ethos = Haltung (attitude); pathos = Befindlichkeit (one's feeling of attunement). Pöggeler reads this as Heidegger SUBSTITUTING an existential-ontological category (Befindlichkeit) for the rhetorical category (pathos), thereby losing the pathos-as-rhetorical-resource that the orator deliberately deploys. The pathetic / pathic is 'relegated' to attunement and mood, and rhetoric's claim on pathos is dissolved into the existential structure of being-in-the-world.

key_concepts.name: Movement as Poiētikon and Pathētikon
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: At the close of GA 18 Heidegger asserts that kinēsis possesses both poiētikon (creativity) and pathētikon (feeling). Pöggeler reads this as Heidegger laying the conceptual track for BT's poiesis-emphasis: the 'destruction of traditional ontology proceeds from its analysis of manual activity' — praxis becomes poiesis (production); pathos is sidelined into Befindlichkeit/Stimmung. Aristotle's praxis-as-rhetorical-communication is restricted to manufactural metaphor.

key_concepts.name: Holy Fear vs. Slavish Fear
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Augustinian distinction (cited via Dilthey's Renaissance-and-Reformation analyses, n. 36): holy fear (timor castus) vs. slavish fear (timor servilis) — fear of God vs. fear of God's punishments in the afterlife. Heidegger imports this Christian theological distinction to read Aristotelian phobos (Rhet. II.5), Pöggeler observes; this is the Christian-theological scaffolding underneath Heidegger's seemingly Aristotelian fear-analysis.

key_concepts.name: Authenticity (Eigentlichkeit) vs. Public-Spirited Rhetorical Tradition
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Pöggeler's most concise diagnosis of Heidegger's dropping-rhetoric move: Heidegger does not consider the polis as the setting for decisions; he treats publicness (Öffentlichkeit) only as the mode of being for 'they' (das Man). Eigentlichkeit, Heidegger's 'most personal character,' is structurally opposed to the public-spirited rhetorical tradition. Heidegger's 1962 Greece trip — imagining himself Heraclitus, never alighting on Patmos, isolated cabin-dweller and Naples-inhabit as contradictory worlds — is the BIOGRAPHICAL allegory of this conceptual choice.

key_concepts.name: Unconcealment (Unverborgenheit) and Self-Concealment
key_concepts.english_form: truth as unconcealment / disclosure of the self-concealed
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's mature truth-of-language concept (cited via Ijsseling): late Heidegger reads truth as 'unconcealment' from a 'strictly non-Platonic and non-metaphysical standpoint,' yet (Ijsseling) the concept 'adheres strictly to the ancient Greek understanding of language' as in Isocrates' panegyric on the power of speech. Pöggeler endorses this reading: the rhetorical tradition is hidden but persistent under Heidegger's mature truth-thinking.

key_concepts.name: Holzwege (Woodpaths) as Deceptive Paths
key_concepts.english_form: woodpaths (paths driven through a wood to carry out timber, ending blind)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Final image of the essay (cited from Ebbinghaus's draft-letter, n. 47): 'Woodpaths do not mean wood paths because wood is an old word for forest, but because they are paths that have been driven through a wood to carry out timber. They end, therefore, blind at the places where timber has been made and are, because of this, paths that deceive the traveler.' Pöggeler uses this as an emblem for Heidegger's late paths: they LOOK like discoveries but end where the timber has been already-made — i.e., where Heidegger's pre-decisions have already foreclosed the rhetorical engagement.

key_concepts.name: Topology vs. Aristotelian Topics
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Pöggeler's structural distinction (note 6 / translator): topos is 'place' or 'position' in Greek; 'topology' is the branch of mathematics that studies 'positions on geometric configurations unaltered by elastic deformation.' Heidegger's metaphorical use of 'topology' suggests properties of Being unchanged by historical or other interpretation — NOT Aristotle's topics, which are commonplaces for argument. Heidegger does NOT follow Aristotelian topics into his Topologie; Vico (rejected by Heidegger) and Viehweg (Topik und Jurisprudenz) develop the Aristotelian topics-tradition, but Heidegger keeps his Topologie distinct.

positions.claim: Heidegger's serious engagement with rhetoric is restricted to the Marburg lecture courses 1923-28; rhetoric is NOT a constitutive concept of his mature thought.
premises: (a) Heidegger's 1947 Aus der Erfahrung des Denkens introduces 'topology of being' as the mature concept; rhetoric is ABSENT from this work and from the Letter on Humanism (1947);

(b) Heidegger's 1957 Der Satz vom Grund explicitly abandons systematic essence-articulation in favor of listening-for-language; the principle of reason is read as terminating-point of metaphysics, NOT as rhetorical commonplace;

(c) Heidegger's 1958 letter to Pöggeler glosses 'topology' as 'speaking of place; thinking the truth' — and explicitly distances his usage from 'historical connotations' (which would include the rhetorical-topical tradition);

(d) The Geviert (fourfold), Trakl essay (1953), and On the Way to Language (1959) develop a place-figure that is poetic, not rhetorical — Heidegger's pivot is to Hölderlin, not to Aristotle's Rhetoric
targets: Gross's titular thesis (HR-01-GROSS-A) that 'Heidegger thus relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology' (Intro p. 4);
Volume-wide assumption (visible in Hyde, Struever, Kisiel) that BT 178 / GA 18 110's 'rhetoric is the first systematic hermeneutic of everydayness' is a load-bearing positive endorsement of rhetoric

positions.claim: On the path to Being and Time, Heidegger restricted CRUCIAL DIMENSIONS of Aristotle's Rhetoric; what looks like an embrace of rhetoric is in fact a CURTAILMENT.
premises: (a) BT §29 reads Aristotle's Rhetoric as 'the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of being amongst one another' — but Heidegger thereby CONFINES the political to everydayness (das Man / Öffentlichkeit), not extending it to deliberative public assembly;

(b) Heidegger glosses pathos with Befindlichkeit, thereby relegating the rhetorical pathē (Aristotle Rhet. II) to existential attunement — the orator's deliberate use of pathos as a resource is dissolved;

(c) When Heidegger 'ceases any longer to set passions and feelings over against virtues,' he leaves behind not only Aristotle but also Scheler — and Nietzsche-style ressentiment-analysis is foreclosed;
(d) Heidegger 'failed to ask' the new-rhetoric question about justice (Perelman) — though it was self-evident for Aristotle and Aquinas
targets: Hyde's reading (HR-04-HYDE) that Heidegger's call of conscience operates 'ontologically as a primordial and emotional form of epideictic rhetoric' — Pöggeler's premise (b) and (c) imply that the BT-§§54-60 conscience-analysis is precisely where rhetoric is LOST, not preserved

Gross's reading (HR-01-GROSS) that pathos is 'the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects' — Pöggeler reads BT §29 as the moment Heidegger SUBSTITUTES Befindlichkeit for pathos

positions.claim: Heidegger's 1923-28 Marburg engagement was rhetorical only because it was a PHILOLOGICAL Aristotle interpretation; the Plato-Aristotle contrast on rhetoric is what Heidegger thematizes, NOT rhetoric itself as a constructive concept.
premises: (a) Heidegger's WS 1925-26 lecture course was renamed FROM 'Aristotle: Rhetoric' TO 'Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy' (GA 18 SS 1924, n. 28) — the rename is itself a restriction;
(b) Heidegger's Sophist course (GA 19) sharpens the Plato-vs-rhetoric opposition: Plato refuses, Aristotle classifies rhetoric under topics within practical philosophy;
(c) Heidegger 'started from a definition of these concepts' — i.e., Aristotle's definitions, not a rhetorical concept built constructively;
(d) Pöggeler's tracking 1947 → 1957 → Marburg → final position shows the Marburg engagement as a temporally bounded EPISODE, not a generative source
targets: Kisiel's reading (HR-06-KISIEL §I-II) that GA 18 originates a 'rhetorical protopolitics' with continuous afterlife;
Michalski's reading (HR-03-MICHALSKI) that GA 18's philological orientation is methodologically SUSTAINING rather than circumscribing

positions.claim: The 1947 Letter on Humanism is the post-rhetorical document par excellence: animal rationale relegates the human to the level of the animal, Hölderlin replaces both Goethe's citizen-of-the-world AND the Romantics, and the polemic against the 'dictatorship of publicness' simultaneously polemicizes against the polis-orientation of rhetoric.
premises: (a) Letter on Humanism's 'first sentence': action (Handeln) is bringing-to-fulfillment (Vollbringen), to be said as poiesis — the distinction between theory and practice falls within the technical interpretation of thought;
(b) Heidegger 'unable to confront the published reports of his actions in 1933' polemicizes against the dictatorship of publicness (Öffentlichkeit) — the same Öffentlichkeit BT had named as das Man;
(c) Heidegger 'understands the humanism of the Renaissance to derive from Rome' (a view Herder rejected) — and 'never queries the significant themes of humanism' or its 'new role to Aristotle';
(d) Heidegger's 1962 Greece-trip biography: imagined as Heraclitus on ship, never alighted on Patmos — the 'isolated cabin dweller and Naples inhabit contradictory worlds'
targets: Anyone (Sartre, Renaissance humanists, Vico, Perelman) who would situate rhetoric as humanism's natural medium
The volume's positive-amplification cluster (Gross, Hyde, Struever, Kisiel) that reads later Heidegger as continuous with the Marburg rhetorical engagement

positions.claim: Even when hidden, Heidegger 'touches the rhetorical tradition again and again' — the relationship is one of buried debt, not of theoretical inheritance.
premises: (a) Heidegger's late discussion (Erörterung) terminology has the rhetorical Aristotelian topics-tradition as its unacknowledged genealogy (Ebbinghaus's draft-letter: erörtern = to carry contemplation through prescribed places (Örter/loci);

(b) Ijsseling: late Heidegger's truth-of-language adheres 'strictly to the ancient Greek understanding of language' as in Isocrates' panegyric — the conflict with rhetoric is itself constitutive of the philosophical tradition's self-limit;

(c) Kuhn (n. 15): topics as theory of place 'held sway from Aristotle and Cicero to Vico' — this is at least 'a first approximation' to Heidegger's discussion; topics 'was to become fundamental ontology' — but Heidegger himself was 'not involved' in this Apel/Hartmann/Viehweg/Vico 'alchemy';
(d) Heidegger's failure to 'further develop this early exploratory path' is REGRETTABLE — Pöggeler's evaluation of the Marburg episode is mournful, not celebratory
targets: (implicit) The volume editors' framing that the Marburg engagement makes Heidegger 'fundamentally rhetorical' through and through

positions.claim: The topology of being (Heidegger's mature concept) is structurally distinct from the rhetorical topics tradition: topology proceeds from Heidegger's December 1958 letter explicating 'speaking of place; thinking the truth' as the disclosure of the self-concealed of being — the figure is poetic-place, not rhetorical-place.
premises: (a) Heidegger's 1958 letter to Pöggeler explicitly bracketed 'historical connotations' of the term 'topology';

(b) Geviert (fourfold) is the geometric figure that crystallizes the topology — the four corners (earth, sky, mortal, gods) cross over Seyn with strikethrough — this is poetic-cosmic, not rhetorical-argumentative;

(c) Heidegger 'lets speak the guiding words of Western thought' (Der Satz vom Grund 1957) — these are GENEALOGICAL guiding-words (the principle of reason), not RHETORICAL Leitworte in Auerbach's sense;
(d) Vico's New Science / De nostris temporis studiorum ratione is rejected by Heidegger as 'Latin and Italian, therefore following the Roman transformation of the legacy of the ancients'
targets: Any reading that conflates Heidegger's Topologie with Aristotelian topics
Any reading that sees the late Heidegger as a continuation of the early-Marburg rhetorical engagement

positions.claim: Pöggeler's silence on BT 178 / GA 18 110 ('rhetoric as first systematic hermeneutic of everydayness') as a load-bearing endorsement is itself a position: he treats this passage NOT as a positive valorization of rhetoric but as the moment Heidegger CONFINES the political to everydayness (das Man) and thereby surrenders the deliberative-public dimension Aristotle's Rhetoric had named.
premises: (a) BT §29 (cited in n. 33): 'Contrary to the traditional orientation of the concept of rhetoric to something like a subject, Aristotle's work must be regarded as the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness (Alltäglichkeit) of being amongst one another' — Pöggeler reads this as RESTRICTIVE, not constitutive;
(b) Heidegger 'does not consider the polis as the setting for decisions, treating publicness (Öffentlichkeit) only as the mode of being for they (das Man)';
(c) Pöggeler asks: 'Does Heidegger assume the political in general to be confined to everydayness and hence just to the businesslike dealings of the they?'
(d) The omission of the rhetorical-deliberative-public dimension is THE RESTRICTION — the title's 'restricted' refers to this omission as much as to the temporal bounding
targets: Hyde, Struever, Gross, Kisiel — all four cite BT 178 / GA 18 110 as load-bearing positive evidence
VT9 in Phase 0: Pöggeler's omission of this passage in Ch 7 is correctly flagged as significant

positions.claim: There is a fundamental temporal asymmetry in how the volume's contributors are reading Heidegger: Pöggeler tracks BACKWARD from 1947 (post-Marburg, post-rhetoric); the other contributors track FORWARD from 1924 (Marburg, rhetorical).
premises: (a) The essay's structural movement is 1947 (Aus der Erfahrung des Denkens) → 1957 (Der Satz vom Grund) → 1958 (letter on topology) → Marburg 1923-28 → final (rhetorical) position;
(b) Pöggeler's choice of starting-point is itself argumentative: opening with 1947 frontloads the topology-of-being concept that displaces rhetoric;
(c) The other six essays open with GA 18 SS 1924 or BT — i.e., with the rhetorical engagement;
(d) The temporal asymmetry produces opposite verdicts on the same loci (BT §29, GA 18 110, Aristotle's Rhetoric)
targets: Volume's structural framing: opens with Gross's centrality thesis, closes with Pöggeler's restriction thesis — the framing disagreement is BAKED INTO the volume's architecture

interlocutors.name: Aristotle
interlocutors.role: Primary object of Heidegger's Marburg engagement; the Rhetoric provides Heidegger with the material for the BT §29 hermeneutic-of-everydayness thesis; Topics is the proper home of rhetoric in Aristotle's classification (Aristotle 'classified rhetoric and its topics among the intellectual disciplines'); the NE VI phronēsis becomes Heidegger's Gewissen
citations: Rhetoric (titular concept; Heidegger's 1924-25 lecture title before rename); Topics (rhetoric classified under); Nicomachean Ethics 1126b12 (communication of words and desires); NE VI (phronēsis); Metaphysics Theta (possibility/actuality); Politics (zōon politikon, polis)
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed → restricted — Heidegger uses Aristotle but curtails the rhetorical-deliberative-public dimension

interlocutors.name: Plato
interlocutors.role: Foil to Aristotle on rhetoric: Plato refuses rhetoric; Aristotle classifies it under topics within practical philosophy; Heidegger sharpens the Plato-rhetoric opposition in his Sophist course (GA 19) but does NOT therefore endorse rhetoric — both Plato and Aristotle, for Heidegger, end up in a 2000-year 'ontology of shoemaking'
citations: GA 19 Plato Sophist (WS 1924/25); Plato Phaedrus (rhetoric position); Plato Statesman (Heidegger's preferred dialogue?, n. 28 area); Plato Sophist
interlocutors.relationship: contrasted via Heidegger; both ultimately eclipsed by Heidegger's late turn to Hölderlin/Heraclitus

interlocutors.name: Husserl
interlocutors.role: The starting point for Heidegger's phenomenology (Heidegger arrives Freiburg 1916); Husserl's transcendental turn (1916+) toward modernity is what Heidegger reverses; Heidegger combined intuition with Bergson's intuition-as-life-flow in his 1919 first postwar lecture; BT (1927) dedicated to Husserl
citations: Husserl Festschrift 1929 (Vom Wesen des Grundes contribution)
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed (phenomenology) → reversed (away from transcendental toward facticity)

interlocutors.name: Wilhelm Dilthey
interlocutors.role: Hermeneutic-of-life proximate source; Introduction to the Human Sciences sees Leibniz and Hegel as final formulators of metaphysical thinking in the principle of reason; Renaissance-and-Reformation analyses inform Heidegger's pathos-via-Christian-tradition reading; Dilthey's Hegel work via Julius Ebbinghaus connects to Heidegger's announced Hermeneutics of Historical Knowledge lectures (Jan 4, 1924)
citations: Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften / Introduction to the Human Sciences (n. 4); Weltanschauung und Analyse des Menschen seit Renaissance und Reformation (n. 36)
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed (hermeneutic-of-life genealogy) — but Heidegger's own hermeneutic absorbs and surpasses Dilthey's

interlocutors.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
interlocutors.role: Heidegger's student; Pöggeler's habilitation supervisor; Truth and Method's reception of rhetoric is a 'topic' (n. 18-19); Gadamer 'had to admit the fact that hermeneutics did not originate during the Reformation, thence universalized by Schleiermacher — it had older roots in the tradition of rhetoric'
citations: Wahrheit und Methode (Truth and Method, n. 19); 'Rhetorik, Hermeneutik und Ideologiekritik' (n. 18); Heidegger und die Griechen (n. 31 area)
interlocutors.relationship: ALLY (Gadamer's late acknowledgment that hermeneutics has older roots in rhetoric supports Pöggeler's broader claim that the rhetorical tradition is hidden but persistent)

interlocutors.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
interlocutors.role: Pivotal figure: Birth of Tragedy §15 names the principle of reason a 'supreme metaphysical delusion'; Nietzsche's listening to the Romantics and their theories of irony connects via Behler to Derrida (Nietzsche the rhetorician); 1938 'conversion year' Heidegger makes Nietzsche jointly responsible for National Socialism; Nietzsche becomes 'most excessive metaphysician' of metaphysics' demise
citations: Die Geburt der Tragödie / Birth of Tragedy §15 (n. 5); Heidegger's 1936-37 Nietzsche lectures; Heidegger's 1938 essays; Pöggeler's own Friedrich Nietzsche und Martin Heidegger (n. 39)
interlocutors.relationship: double role — Nietzsche is BOTH the figure Heidegger uses to cap the metaphysical tradition AND the figure whose rhetoric-attentive side Heidegger fails to honor

interlocutors.name: Max Scheler
interlocutors.role: Heidegger's debt for the realm of the emotional in BT (acknowledged in BT's dedication-area); Scheler 'felt it absurd for Heidegger to presume that Plato and Aristotle had involved Western thought in a two-thousand-year-long ontology of shoemaking'; Scheler's ressentiment-virtue analysis is what Heidegger leaves behind when he ceases to 'set passions over against virtues'
citations: Heidegger's 1928 obituary of Scheler; Pöggeler's 'Ressentiment und Tugend bei Max Scheler' (n. 34)
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed but abandoned by Heidegger; preserved by Pöggeler as a rhetorical-affective register Heidegger restricted

interlocutors.name: Erich Auerbach
interlocutors.role: Mimesis presents 'a version of Western literature and calls it a topology'; Auerbach identifies guiding-words (Leitworte) lexically extractable from texts (e.g., 'la cour et la ville' for the French classics); Auerbach demonstrates a 'particular sort of existential realism' through topical readings
citations: Mimesis: Dargestellte Wirklichkeit in der abendländischen Literatur (n. 8); Vier Untersuchungen zur Geschichte der französischen Bildung (n. 9)
interlocutors.relationship: ally — Auerbach's rhetorical-literary topology is what Pöggeler holds out as the more adequate concept Heidegger left behind

interlocutors.name: Ernst Robert Curtius
interlocutors.role: Speaks of topoi of researching a place (Toposforschung); medieval Latin literary tradition; transmitted ancient tradition (Isidore's importance); Pöggeler observes Curtius (inspired by Bergson rather than Vico) was anti-Cartesian
citations: Europäische Literatur und lateinisches Mittelalter / European Literature and the Latin Middle Ages (n. 7)
interlocutors.relationship: ally for Toposforschung; counter-Cartesian humanism Heidegger did not pursue

interlocutors.name: Giambattista Vico
interlocutors.role: Neapolitan Anti-Cartesian; De nostris temporis studiorum ratione (1708 lecture published 1947 by Helmut Küpper) practices critical methods of Cartesians but reverses them: instead of apodictic, lead arguments (inventio argumentorum); Vico 'spoke as a teacher who brought topics into play'; Vico's Christian Platonism in middle phase (Liber metaphysicus) related back to Aristotle in Truth and Method; Heidegger 'in conversation' with Pöggeler 'would not reconsider a thinker like Vico' — judgment fixed: Vico 'wrote in Latin and Italian, therefore following the Roman transformation of the legacy of the ancients'
citations: De nostris temporis studiorum ratione, ed. Schalk, trans. Otto, Bonn-Bad Godesberg: Küpper, 1947 (n. 14); New Science (n. 20); Vico, Liber metaphysicus, trans. Otto and Viechtbauer (n. 20); Pöggeler's own 'Vico und die humanistische Tradition' (n. 20)
interlocutors.relationship: REJECTED by Heidegger — Pöggeler treats this rejection as conclusive evidence of Heidegger's restriction

interlocutors.name: Theodor Viehweg
interlocutors.role: Topik und Jurisprudenz (1953): early result of Vico's revaluation of topics — practical discipline ranking between metonymy and theology; topology as 'technique for thinking problems' (Hartmann's dialectic); 'ontological bridge' supporting the rhetorical-literary critical preparation
citations: Topik und Jurisprudenz / Topics and Law (n. 13)
interlocutors.relationship: ally — exemplar of post-Aristotelian topics tradition Heidegger did not join

interlocutors.name: Karl-Otto Apel
interlocutors.role: Apel 'dares to pass on this linguistic-philosophical bridge building, especially the Italian humanism of Vico'; in 1968 Kiel address adopts the 'obligation to emancipation in order to validate a quest for an ultimate ground'; Habermas (1963) agreed with Hennis that practical philosophy could establish ties to rhetoric — Pöggeler critiques Apel-Habermas attempts to recover practical philosophy as 'transcendental-pragmatic' (Apel's later term)
citations: Apel, 'Szientistik, Hermeneutik, Ideologiekritik' (n. 17); Apel-edited Transzendentalpragmatik (n. 16, n. 18); Pöggeler's own 'Erklären-Verstehen-Erörtern' (n. 16)
interlocutors.relationship: neighborhood ally; Heidegger 'not involved in this alchemy'

interlocutors.name: Jürgen Habermas
interlocutors.role: 1963 Theorie und Praxis: Habermas agreed with Wilhelm Hennis that practical philosophy could make its own way and could thereby establish ties to the tradition of rhetoric
citations: Theorie und Praxis: Sozialphilosophische Studien (n. 16)
interlocutors.relationship: ally — but Pöggeler's attitude is mixed: Habermas's communicative-rationality program is also implicitly the target of Heidegger's anti-publicness polemic

interlocutors.name: Samuel Ijsseling
interlocutors.role: Has sought to show that the conflict with rhetoric has been constitutive for the philosophical tradition; late Heidegger's truth-of-language regards self-concealments from a 'strictly non-Platonic and non-metaphysical standpoint,' yet 'we cannot fail to recognize that Heidegger's concept adheres strictly to the ancient Greek understanding of language, as it is presented, for example, in Isocrates' panegyric on the power of speech and language'
citations: Rhetorik und Philosophie / Rhetoric and Philosophy in Conflict (n. 44)
interlocutors.relationship: ALLY — Ijsseling's reading directly supports Pöggeler's hidden-but-persistent thesis

interlocutors.name: Julius Ebbinghaus
interlocutors.role: Heidegger's friend (espousing view contrary to his father's, Hermann Ebbinghaus, the empirical psychologist and adversary of Dilthey); Heidegger's January 4, 1924 letter to Ebbinghaus discusses Bultmann and the announced 'Hermeneutics of Historical Knowledge' lectures; later (Nov 22, 1950) Heidegger wrote Ebbinghaus 'to recall walks in the winter landscape of the streets of Freiburg and the Immental Valley'; Ebbinghaus's reply discusses tolerance; the published draft-letter elaborates on erörtern as Aristotelian topics

interlocutors.relationship: Heidegger's correspondent; Pöggeler uses Ebbinghaus's draft-letter as the closing image (Holzwege as deceptive paths)

interlocutors.name: Helmut Kuhn
interlocutors.role: 1970 Gadamer Festschrift essay (with Pöggeler's reply, reprinted in Riedel's Rehabilitierung der praktischen Philosophie vol. 2): topics 'held sway from Aristotle and Cicero to Vico' and may be regarded as 'a first approximation' to Heidegger's discussion; topics 'was to become fundamental ontology'

interlocutors.name: Chaim Perelman

edges.note: Pöggeler's titular thesis: the topology of being (Heidegger's mature post-1947 concept, glossed in his Dec 12, 1958 letter as 'speaking of place; thinking the truth') displaces rhetoric as Heidegger's organizing philosophical category. Note: 'supersedes' is treated here as a domain-specific narrowing of 'undermines' within the controlled vocabulary; the edge captures temporal-conceptual displacement, not contradiction.

Heidegger's Topologie is structurally distinct from the Auerbach-Curtius rhetorical-literary topology; in his Dec 1958 letter Heidegger explicitly disavows 'historical connotations' (which would include the rhetorical-topical tradition); the Geviert (fourfold) is poetic-cosmic not rhetorical-argumentative

Heidegger's Erörterung is the practice of the Topologie: 'discussion (Erörterung) points to place (Ort); and place gathers in and permeates everything' (1953 Trakl essay / 1959 On the Way to Language). The German play on Ort/Erörterung is what Heidegger intends; the topology is performed in Erörterung

Ebbinghaus's draft-letter (n. 47): erörtern = 'to carry contemplation through the places (Örter/loci) prescribed by the topic' — the German verb has the Aristotelian topics-tradition as its hidden genealogy; even Heidegger's late discussion-practice 'touches the rhetorical tradition again and again' (P5)

Heidegger's gloss in GA 18 (ethos = Haltung; pathos = Befindlichkeit) is the moment of conceptual restriction: the rhetorical pathos that the orator deliberately deploys is dissolved into the existential attunement of being-in-the-world. P2 premise (b) makes this explicit; the BT §29 passage on Aristotle's Rhetoric as 'first systematic hermeneutic of everydayness' confirms it

At the close of GA 18, Heidegger asserts kinēsis possesses both poiētikon (creativity) and pathētikon (feeling) — the conceptual track for BT's poiesis-emphasis. The 'pathetic or feeling is relegated to attunement (Befindlichkeit) and mood (Stimmung)' — i.e., rhetoric's pathos is operationalized as existential mood. This IS the restriction in conceptual form

1922 Natorp-Bericht: Heidegger characterizes phronēsis (NE VI) as Gewissen, 'discrediting metaphysical reason.' This is the conceptual hinge: rhetorical-pathic register is channeled into ethical-existential register, restricting rhetoric's distinctive contribution. Pöggeler treats this 1922 move as preparing the BT-§29 restriction (P3)

Pöggeler's structural diagnosis: Heidegger's Eigentlichkeit and the public-spirited rhetorical tradition 'inhabit contradictory worlds' (cabin dweller vs. Naples). Heidegger's choice of authenticity-as-philosophical-existence is structurally opposed to rhetoric's polis-orientation. The 1962 Greece trip (imagined Heraclitus, never alighted on Patmos) is biographical confirmation

Self-loop on the topology concept. Closing image: Heidegger's 'paths' (Holzwege) are paths driven through the wood to carry out timber — they end blind where the timber has been already-made; they 'deceive the traveler.' The topology-of-being is one such path: it appears to discover but in fact ends where Heidegger's pre-decisions (anti-rhetoric, anti-publicness, anti-Vico) have foreclosed the destination

VOLUME-FRAMING DISAGREEMENT (= VT1 in Phase 0): Pöggeler's restriction-thesis ('rhetoric is restricted to the Marburg episode; topology of being supplants rhetoric in mature Heidegger') vs. Gross's centrality-thesis ('Heidegger thus relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology', Intro p. 4). Volume opens with Gross, closes with Pöggeler — the disagreement is built into the volume's architecture

Pöggeler's premise that Heidegger 'restricted crucial dimensions of Aristotle's Rhetoric on the path to Being and Time' — specifically, that ceasing 'any longer to set passions and feelings over against virtues' leaves Aristotle (and Scheler) behind — directly undermines Hyde's reading of BT §§54-60 as 'a primordial and emotional form of epideictic rhetoric.' Pöggeler reads the BT conscience-block as where rhetoric is LOST, not preserved

Pöggeler's reading of GA 18 as a bounded philological-Aristotle interpretation episode contrasts with Kisiel's reading of GA 18 as the genesis of a 'rhetorical protopolitics' with continuous afterlife (Phenomenological → Metontological → Archaic-Poietic). Both cite GA 18; both read the same loci; their verdicts diverge sharply. Partial alignment: Pöggeler's late-Heidegger pivot to Hölderlin/Heraclitus = Kisiel's Phase III 'Archaic-Poietic'

Pöggeler agrees with Michalski's philological framing of GA 18 (Heidegger 'asked philological questions about Aristotle's fundamental concepts'), but RESTRICTS the import: for Michalski the philological orientation is methodologically sustaining; for Pöggeler the philological orientation is part of what makes the Marburg engagement a bounded episode that does not generalize

Pöggeler agrees with Gadamer's late acknowledgment that 'hermeneutics did not originate during the Reformation, thence universalized by Schleiermacher — it had older roots in the tradition of rhetoric'; Pöggeler uses this to ground the broader claim that 'even when it is hidden, Heidegger touches the rhetorical tradition again and again'

VT9 in Phase 0: Pöggeler's reading of BT §29 (= BT 178 / GA 18 110) as RESTRICTIVE rather than constitutive. Hyde, Struever, Gross, Kisiel all read this passage as load-bearing positive evidence; Pöggeler reads it as the moment Heidegger CONFINES the political to everydayness (das Man). Pöggeler's contrastive omission of the GA 18 110 epigraph is itself a position

Volume's structural framing: opens with Gross's centrality-forward-from-1924 thesis, closes with Pöggeler's restriction-backward-from-1947 thesis. The temporal asymmetry produces opposite verdicts on the same loci. The framing disagreement is BAKED INTO the volume's architecture (VT1 in Phase 0)
Aus der Erfahrung des Denkens (1947) is where 'topology of being' is introduced; the dwelling-place (Ortschaft) of essence; thoughtful poetics. The 1947 publication is the temporal pivot of the essay

Heidegger's own self-interpretation: 'I use the term "topology" quite literally: the speaking of place; that is, thinking the truth (the disclosure of the self-concealed [das Entbergen des Sichverbergens]) of being [des Seyns]. In using this term I was not aware of the historical connotations you have suggested.' This is the locus where Heidegger explicitly disavows the rhetorical-historical genealogy

BT §29 reads Aristotle's Rhetoric as 'first systematic hermeneutic of everydayness'; Pöggeler reads this as the moment of restriction (P2, P7). The Aristotelian pathē of fear (Rhet. II.5) are absorbed into Befindlichkeit as a mood-structure of being-in-the-world

At the close of GA 18, Heidegger's reading of Aristotle's De anima III on kinēsis (with poiētikon and pathētikon) provides the conceptual frame for BT's poiesis-emphasis and the relegation of pathos to Befindlichkeit

Letter on Humanism (1947) is the post-rhetorical document: polemic against 'dictatorship of publicness' (Öffentlichkeit), against humanism's Aristotle, against Vico/Renaissance — the explicit programmatic restriction of the rhetorical-public dimension
1922 Natorp-Bericht: Heidegger characterizes phronēsis (NE VI) as Gewissen — the conceptual hinge that channels rhetorical-pathic register into BT existential-ethical register

Heidegger's SS 1924 lecture course (originally announced as 'Aristotle: Rhetoric,' renamed 'Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy') presupposes the Aristotelian classification of rhetoric under topics within practical philosophy. Pöggeler treats the rename itself as evidence of the restriction

Vico's De nostris temporis studiorum ratione (1708 lecture, published 1947 by Küpper) practices critical methods of Cartesians but reverses them via topical inventio; Heidegger 'in conversation with Pöggeler would not reconsider a thinker like Vico' — judgment fixed: Vico 'wrote in Latin and Italian, therefore following the Roman transformation of the legacy of the ancients.' This biographical refusal is, for Pöggeler, conclusive evidence of restriction

Auerbach's Mimesis presents 'a version of Western literature and calls it a topology'; identifies guiding-words (Leitworte) lexically extractable from texts (e.g., 'la cour et la ville' for the French classics). This is the rhetorical-literary topology Pöggeler holds out as the more adequate concept Heidegger's Topologie partly inhabits without acknowledging

Ijsseling (Rhetoric and Philosophy in Conflict): late Heidegger's truth-of-language regards self-concealments from a 'strictly non-Platonic and non-metaphysical standpoint,' yet 'Heidegger's concept adheres strictly to the ancient Greek understanding of language, as it is presented in Isocrates' panegyric on the power of speech.' Pöggeler endorses this reading: the rhetorical tradition is hidden but persistent

Heidegger 'failed to ask' the new-rhetoric question about justice (Perelman's La nouvelle rhétorique 1958) — though it was self-evident for Aristotle and Aquinas. The question Heidegger doesn't ask is the test he fails. Pöggeler's verdict on the Marburg engagement
